papers.title: All Languages Matter: On the Multilingual Safety of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Safety lies at the core of developing and deploying large language models (LLMs). However, previous safety benchmarks only concern the safety in one language, e.g. the majority language in the pretraining data such as English. In this work, we build the first multilingual safety benchmark for LLMs, XSafety, in response to the global deployment of LLMs in practice. XSafety covers 14 kinds of commonly used safety issues across 10 languages that span several language families. We utilize XSafety to empirically study the multilingual safety for 4 widely-used LLMs, including both close-API and open-source models. Experimental results show that all LLMs produce significantly more unsafe responses for non-English queries than English ones, indicating the necessity of developing safety alignment for non-English languages. In addition, we propose several simple and effective prompting methods to improve the multilingual safety of ChatGPT by evoking safety knowledge and improving cross-lingual generalization of safety alignment. Our prompting method can significantly reduce the ratio of unsafe responses from 19.1% to 9.7% for non-English queries. We release our data at https://github.com/Jarviswang94/Multilingual_safety_benchmark.

papers.title: Safety Assessment of Chinese Large Language Models
papers.abstract: With the rapid popularity of large language models such as ChatGPT and GPT-4, a growing amount of attention is paid to their safety concerns. These models may generate insulting and discriminatory content, reflect incorrect social values, and may be used for malicious purposes such as fraud and dissemination of misleading information. Evaluating and enhancing their safety is particularly essential for the wide application of large language models (LLMs). To further promote the safe deployment of LLMs, we develop a Chinese LLM safety assessment benchmark. Our benchmark explores the comprehensive safety performance of LLMs from two perspectives: 8 kinds of typical safety scenarios and 6 types of more challenging instruction attacks. Our benchmark is based on a straightforward process in which it provides the test prompts and evaluates the safety of the generated responses from the evaluated model. In evaluation, we utilize the LLM's strong evaluation ability and develop it as a safety evaluator by prompting. On top of this benchmark, we conduct safety assessments and analyze 15 LLMs including the OpenAI GPT series and other well-known Chinese LLMs, where we observe some interesting findings. For example, we find that instruction attacks are more likely to expose safety issues of all LLMs. Moreover, to promote the development and deployment of safe, responsible, and ethical AI, we publicly release SafetyPrompts including 100k augmented prompts and responses by LLMs.

papers.title: Safety at Scale: A Comprehensive Survey of Large Model and Agent Safety
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of large models, driven by their exceptional abilities in learning and generalization through large-scale pre-training, has reshaped the landscape of Artificial Intelligence (AI). These models are now foundational to a wide range of applications, including conversational AI, recommendation systems, autonomous driving, content generation, medical diagnostics, and scientific discovery. However, their widespread deployment also exposes them to significant safety risks, raising concerns about robustness, reliability, and ethical implications. This survey provides a systematic review of current safety research on large models, covering Vision Foundation Models (VFMs), Large Language Models (LLMs), Vision-Language Pre-training (VLP) models, Vision-Language Models (VLMs), Diffusion Models (DMs), and large-model-powered Agents. Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We present a comprehensive taxonomy of safety threats to these models, including adversarial attacks, data poisoning, backdoor attacks, jailbreak and prompt injection attacks, energy-latency attacks, data and model extraction attacks, and emerging agent-specific threats. (2) We review defense strategies proposed for each type of attacks if available and summarize the commonly used datasets and benchmarks for safety research. (3) Building on this, we identify and discuss the open challenges in large model safety, emphasizing the need for comprehensive safety evaluations, scalable and effective defense mechanisms, and sustainable data practices. More importantly, we highlight the necessity of collective efforts from the research community and international collaboration. Our work can serve as a useful reference for researchers and practitioners, fostering the ongoing development of comprehensive defense systems and platforms to safeguard AI models.

papers.title: Enhanced Diagnostic and Interpretable Model for Febrile Diseases Using Explainable AI and Large Language Model
papers.abstract: <p><span>Tropical febrile diseases pose significant public health challenges in tropical regions, particularly in resource-limited settings, where timely and accurate diagnoses are critical for effective disease management. However, existing diagnostic systems are black-box and often lack interpretability, making it difficult for healthcare practitioners to understand and trust machine learning (ML) predictions. Additionally, the existing system excludes younger patients, limiting its applicability. This study aimed to develop an integrated diagnostic system that enhances interpretability by leveraging machine learning (ML), Explainable AI (XAI), and a large language model (LLM). A dataset comprising 3,914 patient records with 32 symptoms was obtained from a New Frontiers in Research Fund-sponsored project and preprocessed for analysis. Random Forest (RF) was trained with hyperparameter tuning using GridSearchCV and evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation to optimize its performance. The tuned model achieved high diagnostic performance, demonstrating its effectiveness in diagnosing six febrile diseases. To enhance interpretability, a Model Interpretability Framework (MIF) was incorporated, integrating Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) for visual insights and ChatGPT for textual explanations. This combination provided users with a clear understanding of the diagnostic process, addressing the limitations of black-box ML models. The system was implemented using Python in a development environment that included Google Colaboratory, Visual Studio Code, Flet, and MySQL for database management. Agile development methodology and Unified Modeling Language tools were employed to create a user-friendly design for clinicians and patients. The diagnostic system was evaluated using precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC metrics. The RF model achieved outstanding precision for most diseases, high recall (≥0.97), and an AUC-ROC of 0.99, indicating nearly flawless training performance with few misclassifications. On the test dataset, the model performed better in diagnosing malaria (F1-score = 88%, precision = 85%), urinary tract infection (F1-score = 72%, precision = 80%), and respiratory tract infection (F1-score = 72%, precision = 77%). The evaluated system demonstrated strong predictive performance, correctly identifying 72 out of 99 tested patient cases, with 26 cases misclassified and one case completely missed. It achieved the highest detection rates for Malaria and HIV/AIDS, accurately identifying all cases without false positives. This work enhances diagnostic solutions for tropical healthcare settings by improving explainability and ensuring inclusivity for younger patients, addressing key limitations in existing systems. The integration of ML, XAI, and LLM enhances diagnostic performance and lays the groundwork for future AI-driven healthcare innovations, ultimately improving health outcomes in resource-scarce regions. Healthcare providers should adopt this system to enhance the efficiency of disease diagnosis and extend the system to diagnose additional medical conditions.&nbsp;</span></p>

literature_themes.theme: Safety Assessment and Enhancement of Large Language Models
literature_themes.summary: This cluster of papers focuses on the safety concerns associated with large language models (LLMs), particularly in multilingual contexts. It introduces benchmarks for assessing safety in various languages, highlights the increased risks for non-English queries, and explores the safety performance of Chinese LLMs. Additionally, it provides a comprehensive survey of safety threats and defense mechanisms for large models, emphasizing the need for robust safety measures across diverse applications.
literature_themes.limitations: The studies primarily address safety in specific languages or contexts, which may not be generalizable to all languages or scenarios. There is also a lack of comprehensive evaluation frameworks that cover all potential safety threats and the effectiveness of proposed safety enhancements across different LLMs.
literature_themes.gap_relevance: This cluster identifies critical gaps in the current understanding of multilingual safety in LLMs and the need for standardized safety benchmarks. It highlights the importance of developing safety measures that are effective across various languages and applications, thus guiding future research in enhancing the safety and reliability of AI systems.

literature_themes.limitations: The cluster lacks comprehensive empirical evaluations and may not address the scalability of the proposed methods in diverse real-world scenarios. Additionally, the absence of an abstract for one of the papers limits the understanding of its contributions.
literature_themes.gap_relevance: This cluster highlights the need for further research into the practical applications and limitations of using language models in recommendation systems, identifying gaps in the current methodologies that could be explored in future studies.

summary: The literature on interpretable internal representations for enhanced safety in large language models (LLMs) highlights significant safety concerns, particularly in multilingual contexts, and emphasizes the need for standardized safety benchmarks. Studies reveal that LLMs exhibit increased risks for non-English queries and propose methodologies for safety improvement, while also addressing the limitations of existing frameworks. Additionally, research into few-shot recommender systems suggests that LLMs can enhance representation learning, although empirical evaluations are lacking. Overall, the findings underscore the necessity for comprehensive safety evaluations and the integration of interpretability in AI applications.
scholarly_positioning: Existing research on large language models (LLMs) has predominantly focused on safety assessments within specific languages, particularly English, leaving significant gaps in multilingual safety evaluations and the generalizability of findings across diverse contexts. While methodologies for safety improvement have been proposed, they often lack comprehensive frameworks that address all potential threats and empirical validations across various LLMs. Moreover, the integration of interpretability within safety measures remains underexplored, particularly in high-stakes applications. This proposed research aims to bridge these gaps by developing interpretable internal representations that enhance both safety and controllability in LLMs, thereby contributing to a more robust understanding of AI safety in multilingual and diverse settings.
research_scope: This study will focus on the safety and interpretability of large language models (LLMs) within the context of multilingual safety assessments. The target population will include four widely-used LLMs, evaluated across ten languages, with a specific emphasis on non-English queries. The AI intervention will involve the development of a multilingual safety benchmark (XSafety) and the implementation of prompting methods to enhance safety. The evaluation period will span six months, during which model-level safety metrics and human evaluations will be conducted. The primary outcome will be the reduction in unsafe responses across languages, while secondary outcomes will include user trust calibration measures and the effectiveness of interpretability methods in explaining model decisions. Baseline comparisons will be made against existing safety benchmarks and prior evaluation frameworks.
concept_definition:
{
  "Large Language Models (LLMs)": "Advanced AI models capable of understanding and generating human language, specifically evaluated in this study are four widely-used LLMs across ten languages.",
  "Interpretability": "The degree to which the internal workings of LLMs can be understood, focusing on methods like probing, attribution, and attention visualization to clarify model decisions.",
  "Internal Representations": "The hidden states or internal activations of LLMs that capture information processed by the model, which can be analyzed for interpretability.",
  "Safety Outcomes": {
    "Unsafe Response Rate": "The frequency of harmful or inappropriate responses generated by LLMs.",
    "Over-refusal": "Instances where the model refuses to answer questions unnecessarily, potentially limiting its usability.",
    "Jailbreak Success": "The ability of users to manipulate the model into producing unsafe outputs despite safety measures.",
    "Harmful Compliance": "The model's tendency to comply with harmful prompts or requests.",
    "Refusal Precision/Recall": "Metrics evaluating the accuracy of the model's refusals in response to harmful queries."
  },
  "User Trust": {
    "Trust Calibration": "The alignment between a user's perceived trust in the model and the model's actual performance.",
    "Blind Trust": "Trust in the model without understanding its limitations or capabilities.",
    "Perceived Transparency": "How transparent users feel the model is regarding its decision-making processes.",
    "Appropriate Reliance": "The extent to which users depend on the model's outputs based on its reliability and safety."
  },
  "Safety Monitor": "A mechanism or framework used to assess and ensure the safety of LLM outputs during evaluation.",
  "Explanation Generation": "The process of creating understandable justifications for the model's outputs, aimed at researchers, systems, or end-users.",
  "Multilingual Safety Benchmark (XSafety)": "A comprehensive evaluation framework designed to assess the safety of LLMs across multiple languages and contexts, addressing existing gaps in English-centric evaluations."
}
technical_feasibility: The study requires open-source model access for hidden state extraction, labelled datasets for multilingual safety assessments, multilingual prompt sets for diverse evaluations, native-speaker validation for accurate assessments, human participants for trust calibration measures, and ethics approval for human-subject research. Additionally, GPU resources will be necessary for model evaluations and annotation protocols for systematic data collection. If only API models are available, the design should shift towards output-level explanation or black-box evaluation methods, which would eliminate the need for hidden state access. A feasible adjustment would be to focus on output-level interpretability while still conducting user trust studies with available models.
gap: Develop a comprehensive multilingual safety benchmark that evaluates the safety of large language models (LLMs) across diverse languages and contexts, addressing the inadequacies of existing frameworks that primarily focus on English.
question: How does the implementation of a multilingual safety benchmark (XSafety) affect the unsafe response rate of four widely-used large language models (LLMs) across ten languages, particularly for non-English queries, compared to existing English-centric safety frameworks?
theoretical_mechanism: The independent variable is the implementation of the multilingual safety benchmark (XSafety), which serves as a technical mechanism to enhance the safety of LLMs. The mediator in this causal chain is the internal representations of the models, which are influenced by the benchmark and subsequently affect system-level outcomes such as unsafe response rate and refusal accuracy. The moderator is the language context, particularly focusing on non-English queries, which may alter the effectiveness of the safety measures. The dependent variables include the unsafe response rate and refusal precision/recall. The theoretical framework is grounded in safety evaluation and interpretability, suggesting that improved internal representations lead to better safety outcomes through enhanced detection and filtering mechanisms. User-level outcomes, such as trust and reliance, are mediated by perceived transparency and calibrated trust, which are influenced by the interpretability of the model's outputs. Assumptions requiring empirical validation include the effectiveness of the benchmark across diverse languages and the relationship between interpretability and user trust in multilingual contexts.
hypothesis: Implementing the multilingual safety benchmark (XSafety) will significantly reduce the unsafe response rate of large language models (LLMs) for non-English queries compared to existing English-centric safety frameworks.

proposal: This research proposal aims to develop a multilingual safety benchmark (XSafety) to evaluate the safety of large language models (LLMs) across ten languages, focusing on non-English queries, addressing the critical gap in existing literature that predominantly centers on English-centric safety assessments. The core concepts include interpretable internal representations, defined as the hidden states of LLMs that can be analyzed for safety outcomes, and user trust calibration, which measures the alignment between user perceptions and model performance. Technical feasibility assumes access to open-source models, labeled multilingual datasets, and human participants for evaluations. The motivation stems from significant safety concerns in multilingual contexts, as highlighted by recent studies showing increased unsafe response rates for non-English queries. Existing frameworks lack comprehensive evaluations across diverse languages, necessitating the proposed research. The research question investigates how implementing XSafety affects the unsafe response rate of four widely-used LLMs compared to existing frameworks, with a theoretical mechanism positing that XSafety enhances internal representations (independent variable), leading to improved safety outcomes (system-level) and increased user trust (user-level). The falsifiable hypothesis states that implementing XSafety will significantly reduce the unsafe response rate for non-English queries. Constructs will be operationalized using metrics such as unsafe response rates, refusal precision/recall, and user trust calibration measures, with methodologies involving benchmark evaluations, multilingual annotation, and human evaluations. The study will include appropriate controls, such as baseline comparisons against existing safety benchmarks, and will ensure the validity of metrics through rigorous statistical analysis. Expected contributions encompass theoretical advancements in interpretability, technical development of XSafety, empirical insights into safety metrics, and practical deployment guidelines for enhancing LLM safety. Key limitations include potential biases in human evaluations and the challenge of generalizing findings beyond the tested languages, along with risks of misinterpretation of results and ethical concerns regarding LLM misuse.
